materials.title: Reporting lost luggage
materials.instructions: You will hear a passenger reporting a missing suitcase at an airport.
materials.audioScript:
OFFICER: Good evening, baggage services. How can I help?
PASSENGER: Hi. I've just arrived from Singapore and my suitcase didn't come out on the belt.
OFFICER: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me take some details. What's your flight number?
PASSENGER: It's SQ two-one-eight.
OFFICER: Thank you. And your full name?
PASSENGER: Arjun Mehta. That's M-E-H-T-A.
OFFICER: Could you describe the suitcase?
PASSENGER: It's a large hard-shell case, dark green, with four wheels. There's a yellow ribbon tied to the handle.
OFFICER: Any name tag?
PASSENGER: Yes, a leather one with my address on it.
OFFICER: Good, that helps. What's in the case, roughly?
PASSENGER: Mostly clothes, and some books. Oh, and my laptop charger, which I really need.
OFFICER: OK. Where are you staying in the city?
PASSENGER: At the Riverside Hotel, on Albert Street.
OFFICER: And a phone number?
PASSENGER: It's 07700 913 482.
OFFICER: Thank you. Most delayed bags arrive on the next flight from the same city, which lands tomorrow at eleven a.m. If it's on that flight, we'll deliver it to your hotel by the evening, free of charge.
PASSENGER: That's a relief. Can I buy anything I need tonight?
OFFICER: Yes. The airline will refund up to sixty pounds for essential items, such as toiletries. Just keep your receipts and send them with the claim form.
PASSENGER: And how do I check progress?
OFFICER: Use this reference number on our website: GT four-seven-five-nine.

materials.title: Marathon volunteer briefing
materials.instructions: You will hear a coordinator briefing volunteers for a city marathon.
materials.audioScript:
COORDINATOR: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at this year's City Marathon. I'll explain where the main stations are and what each team will be doing on race day.
COORDINATOR: The race starts in Victoria Park. Runners collect their numbers from the registration tents at the north gate, and that's where Team A will be working from six in the morning. Your main job is checking runners' identification, so please be patient, because queues build up quickly.
COORDINATOR: Team B will be at the first water station, which is beside the old bridge, about five kilometres into the course. You'll be handing out water in paper cups. We've stopped using plastic bottles this year, so please make sure runners drop their cups into the recycling bins.
COORDINATOR: Team C will be at the medical tent near the finish line in Market Square. You won't be treating anyone yourselves; that's the job of the paramedics. Instead, you'll be helping to keep the area clear and directing family members to the waiting area.
COORDINATOR: Team D is the baggage team. You'll be at the sports centre, where runners leave their bags before the start. Each bag gets a coloured label matching the runner's number, and runners collect them after the race.
COORDINATOR: A couple of general points. Every volunteer receives an orange jacket, which you must wear at all times, and a free lunch voucher, which you can use at any café on the high street. Please arrive at least thirty minutes before your shift. If you can't come, ring the volunteer hotline rather than sending an email, because nobody will be checking emails on the day.

materials.title: Presentation on social media and sleep
materials.instructions: You will hear two students, Noor and Felix, discussing their presentation with their tutor.
materials.audioScript:
TUTOR: So, Noor and Felix, you're presenting on social media and sleep. How's the research going?
NOOR: Quite well. We've read about a dozen studies. Most of them found that teenagers who use their phones in the hour before bed sleep less, but the effect is smaller than the headlines suggest.
TUTOR: Interesting. What did you find surprising?
FELIX: That it isn't mainly the light from the screen. Several studies suggest the bigger problem is that the content keeps people awake, like messages they feel they have to reply to.
TUTOR: Good. And how are you going to present that?
NOOR: We were going to show a long table of all the studies, but it's probably too much detail for a ten-minute presentation.
TUTOR: I agree. A simple chart comparing two or three key studies would work better. You can put the full table in the handout.
FELIX: OK. We also ran our own small survey of students in our hall.
TUTOR: How many responses?
FELIX: Forty-two. Most said they check their phone after midnight at least three times a week.
TUTOR: That's useful, but be careful. Forty-two students in one hall isn't a representative sample, so you'll need to mention that limitation.
NOOR: Right. And for the ending, we thought we'd give some practical advice.
TUTOR: Such as?
NOOR: Charging phones outside the bedroom. One study found that was more effective than using night-mode settings.
TUTOR: That's a strong way to finish. Who's speaking first?
FELIX: I'll introduce the topic, Noor will cover the research, and I'll come back for our survey and the advice.
TUTOR: Fine. Practise with a timer. Last year many groups went over the limit.

materials.title: Lecture: how desert plants survive
materials.instructions: You will hear part of a lecture about desert plants.
materials.audioScript:
LECTURER: Today we're looking at how plants survive in deserts, where rain may fall only a few times a year and temperatures on the ground can exceed sixty degrees.
LECTURER: Broadly, desert plants use three strategies. The first is to avoid the drought altogether. Many desert annuals spend most of their lives as seeds, which can lie in the soil for years. When heavy rain finally falls, they germinate, flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks, before the ground dries out again.
LECTURER: The second strategy is to store water. Cacti are the best-known example. Their thick stems hold water, and a waxy coating on the surface reduces evaporation. Instead of leaves, most cacti have spines, which lose far less water and also protect the plant from animals. Some cacti can expand their stems like an accordion after rain.
LECTURER: The third strategy is to reach water that other plants cannot. The mesquite tree, for example, has roots that can grow more than forty metres deep to reach groundwater. Other plants do the opposite: they have shallow but very wide root systems that absorb light rain before it evaporates.
LECTURER: Many desert plants also have a special form of photosynthesis. Normally plants open small pores in their leaves during the day to take in carbon dioxide, but this lets water escape. Cacti and some other species open their pores only at night, when it is cooler, store the carbon dioxide, and use it for photosynthesis the following day. This can reduce water loss by as much as ninety per cent.
LECTURER: These adaptations are attracting interest from agricultural scientists, who hope to develop crops that need less irrigation as droughts become more common.

materials.title: The story of paper money
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on the questions based on this passage.
materials.passage:
A For most of history, money meant objects with value of their own: grain, cattle, shells, and above all, precious metals. Coins made of gold, silver or bronze could be weighed and tested, and their worth did not depend on trusting the person who handed them over. The idea that a piece of paper might be accepted as payment would have seemed strange to most people in the ancient world.

B Paper money first appeared in China. During the Tang dynasty, in the ninth century, merchants who travelled long distances began leaving their heavy iron and copper coins with trusted agents and receiving written certificates in return. These certificates, sometimes called "flying money" because they could travel more easily than coins, could be exchanged for coins in another city.

C In the early eleventh century, the government of the Song dynasty took control of this system and began issuing official paper notes. At first, the notes could be exchanged for coins at any time. Over time, however, governments printed more notes than they could support, especially to pay for wars, and the value of the notes fell sharply. Later dynasties experienced similar problems, and by the fifteenth century China had largely stopped using paper money.

D European travellers were astonished by Chinese paper money. In Europe, paper banknotes developed much later, in the seventeenth century, when banks in Sweden and England began issuing notes that represented deposits of gold or silver. A holder could, in principle, take the note to the bank and receive the metal. This link to precious metal gave people confidence that the paper was worth something.

E During the twentieth century, this link was gradually broken. Most countries abandoned the gold standard, and today the value of a banknote depends on public confidence in the government and central bank that issue it. Economists call this "fiat money", from a Latin word meaning "let it be done". The system works as long as people trust that the money will be accepted by others and will not lose its value too quickly.

F Today, paper money itself is declining. In several countries, a large majority of payments are made by card or phone, and some shops no longer accept cash at all. Yet the basic principle that first appeared in China more than a thousand years ago remains the same: money is valuable because people agree that it is.

materials.title: Why do we yawn?
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on the questions based on this passage.
materials.passage:
A Everyone yawns, and almost everyone finds it hard not to yawn when they see someone else do it. Yet despite its familiarity, yawning is still not fully understood. Humans begin yawning before birth, as early as eleven weeks after conception, and the behaviour is found in almost all vertebrates, from fish to birds to mammals.

B For a long time, the most popular explanation was that yawning increases the amount of oxygen in the blood. This idea has largely been abandoned. In experiments in the 1980s, people who breathed air with extra oxygen yawned no less often than usual, and those who breathed air with extra carbon dioxide yawned no more often.

C A more recent theory proposes that yawning helps to cool the brain. A deep yawn draws in a large amount of air and increases blood flow in the face and skull. Supporting this idea, one study found that people yawned less often when they held a cold pack to their forehead than when they held a warm one. Other research has found that people yawn more in moderate temperatures than in very hot or very cold conditions.

D Yawning is also linked to changes in alertness. People yawn most often shortly after waking and before going to sleep, and athletes and performers are often seen yawning just before an important event. Some researchers suggest that yawning helps the brain shift from one state to another, for example from boredom to alertness.

E Perhaps the most intriguing feature of yawning is that it is contagious. Simply seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can trigger a yawn. Studies have found that people are more likely to catch a yawn from a family member or friend than from a stranger, which has led some scientists to link contagious yawning to empathy. Children under about four years old rarely catch yawns, which may reflect the gradual development of social awareness.

F Contagious yawning has also been seen in some other animals, including chimpanzees and dogs. In one study, dogs yawned more often after watching their owners yawn than after watching strangers. Whether this reflects true empathy or simply a reaction to familiar faces remains a matter of debate.

options: An explanation that failed the test
A possible role in temperature control

materials.title: The homework question
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on the questions based on this passage.
materials.passage:
Every few years, the debate about homework returns. Some parents complain that their children spend whole evenings on worksheets, while others worry that schools are not demanding enough. Several schools have abolished homework altogether for younger pupils, and their example is often cited as evidence that homework is unnecessary. In my view, this conclusion goes too far, but the critics have a point.

The research on homework is more mixed than either side tends to admit. For secondary school students, there is reasonable evidence that moderate amounts of homework are associated with better results. For primary school children, however, the evidence of any academic benefit is weak. This does not prove that homework is useless for young children, but it does suggest that hours of written exercises are hard to justify.

What matters more than quantity is the type of work. Homework that asks students to practise something they have already learned in class, such as reading or recalling vocabulary, is likely to help. Homework that requires them to learn new material alone, without the teacher's support, is far less effective, and it disadvantages children whose parents cannot help them. In this sense, poorly designed homework can widen the gap between children from different backgrounds.

There is also the question of time. Children need time to play, rest and pursue their own interests, and these activities have value that is not measured in test scores. A ten-year-old who spends two hours every evening on homework may be losing something important. Yet abolishing homework entirely would also remove a useful opportunity for older students to develop habits of independent study, which they will need at university and work.

The most sensible approach, I believe, is to set limits and to focus on purpose. A short daily period of reading for younger children, and carefully designed practice tasks for older students, would keep the benefits of homework while reducing its costs. Schools should also explain to parents why particular tasks are set. Homework that has a clear purpose is far easier to defend than homework that is set simply because it always has been.

Hillside Leisure Centre: Swimming Pool Information

Opening times
Monday to Friday: 6.30 a.m. to 9.30 p.m.

materials.title: New employee FAQ: pay and benefits
materials.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.
materials.passage:
New employee FAQ: pay and benefits

When will I be paid?
Salaries are paid on the last working day of each month directly into your bank account. Your first payment may be smaller or larger than usual, depending on the date you started.

Where can I see my payslip?
Payslips are not sent by post. You can view and download them from the staff portal two days before each payday.

What if my pay is wrong?
Contact the payroll team within ten working days of payday. Please include your employee number in all messages.

Do you offer a pension?
Yes. All employees are enrolled in the company pension scheme automatically after three months. You contribute 5% of your salary and the company adds 7%. You can choose to leave the scheme, but you will lose the company's contribution.

What other benefits are there?
Staff receive a discount of 20% in the company's shops and cafés. After six months, you can join the cycle-to-work scheme, which lets you buy a bicycle and spread the cost over twelve months. We also offer free, confidential counselling through an external provider.

Can I work flexible hours?
Requests for flexible working can be made after you have completed your probation period of six months. Speak to your line manager first.

materials.title: The return of the tram
materials.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
materials.passage:
A In the first half of the twentieth century, trams ran through the streets of hundreds of cities around the world. By the 1960s, many of these systems had disappeared. Cars and buses seemed more modern and flexible, and tram tracks were seen as an obstacle to traffic. In Britain, for example, almost every city tram system had closed by the early 1960s.

B Over the past forty years, however, the tram has returned. Cities across Europe, as well as in Asia, Australia and North America, have built new tram networks, often reusing the routes of the old ones. The modern versions are usually called light rail or simply trams, and they differ considerably from their predecessors.

C Today's trams are quieter, faster and much more comfortable. Most have low floors, so passengers with wheelchairs, buggies or heavy shopping can board easily from the platform without steps. Many routes have their own lanes or tracks, separated from other traffic, which makes journeys more reliable than bus services that can be delayed by congestion.

D Environmental concerns have been an important reason for their revival. Trams run on electricity, so they produce no exhaust fumes in city streets, and if the power comes from renewable sources, their overall emissions are low. Planners also hope that a high-quality tram service will persuade drivers to leave their cars at home in a way that buses often fail to do.

E Trams are not without drawbacks. Building a new line is expensive and can cause years of disruption to businesses along the route. Critics argue that the same money could provide a much larger network of buses. Supporters reply that trams attract more passengers and encourage investment in the areas they serve, and that a tram line, unlike a bus route, gives businesses confidence that the service is permanent.

F Some cities are now testing a compromise: battery-powered trams that can run without overhead wires on certain sections, and "trackless trams", which look like trams but run on rubber tyres along painted lines. Whether these will replace traditional trams remains to be seen.

groups.instructions: The passage has six paragraphs, A–F. Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F

groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage? Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.prompt: Most British city tram systems had closed by the early 1960s.
New tram lines never follow old routes.
questions.explanation: They often reuse the routes of the old ones.

questions.prompt: Trackless trams run on rubber tyres.
Tram fares are usually higher than bus fares.

materials.title: International students in three countries (line graph)
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
materials.prompt:
The graph below shows the number of international students enrolled at universities in three countries between 2005 and 2025.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
materials.imageAlt: Line graph, thousands of international students. Country P: 120, 165, 210, 190, 260 (2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025). Country Q: 90, 100, 130, 150, 175. Country R: 40, 70, 115, 105, 150.
materials.scoringGuidance: Overview: all three countries ended with more students than they started; Country P remained the largest throughout, and Country R grew fastest proportionally (almost four-fold). P and R dipped in 2020 while Q rose steadily every period. Good answers use accurate figures to support these trends without listing every point.

materials.title: Smartphone ownership by age (bar chart)
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
materials.prompt:
The chart below shows the percentage of people in different age groups who owned a smartphone in one country in 2012 and 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
materials.imageAlt: Bar chart, smartphone ownership 2012 and 2024. Ages 16–24: 78% and 97%. 25–34: 70% and 96%. 35–54: 52% and 92%. 55–64: 30% and 81%. 65 and over: 12% and 63%.
materials.scoringGuidance: Overview: ownership rose in every age group, and the gap between young and old narrowed considerably; ownership falls with age in both years. The biggest increases were among older groups (65+ rose more than five-fold). Strong answers compare the gap between the youngest and oldest groups in each year.
materials.modelAnswer:
The bar chart compares the proportion of people in five age groups who owned a smartphone in one country in 2012 and 2024.

Overall, smartphone ownership increased in every age group over the period, and although younger people were more likely to own one in both years, the gap between the youngest and oldest groups narrowed considerably.

In 2012, ownership was highest among 16 to 24-year-olds, at 78%, and fell steadily with age, to 52% of those aged 35 to 54 and only 12% of people aged 65 and over. By 2024, almost all young adults owned a smartphone, with figures of 97% and 96% for the two youngest groups, and the figure for 35 to 54-year-olds had risen to 92%.

The most dramatic growth occurred among older people. Ownership among 55 to 64-year-olds increased from 30% to 81%, while the proportion of people aged 65 and over rose more than five-fold, to 63%. As a result, the difference between the youngest and oldest groups fell from 66 percentage points in 2012 to 34 points in 2024.

materials.title: Letter: complaint to a gym
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows: Dear Sir or Madam,
materials.prompt:
You are a member of a gym, but you are unhappy with some recent changes.

Write a letter to the manager of the gym. In your letter:
bullets: explain how long you have been a member and why you joined
describe the changes you are unhappy about
say what you would like the manager to do
materials.scoringGuidance: Formal register (Dear Sir or Madam / Yours faithfully). Changes should be specific (reduced opening hours, fewer classes, higher fees) and linked to the reason the writer joined. The request should be realistic, for example restoring a class or offering a partial refund.

materials.title: Letter: organising a farewell for a colleague
materials.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows: Dear …,
materials.prompt:
A colleague who has worked with you for many years is leaving the company. You are organising a farewell event.

Write a letter to another colleague. In your letter:
bullets: explain why you want to organise the event
describe your plans for the event
ask your colleague to help in a particular way
materials.scoringGuidance: Semi-formal or friendly tone between colleagues. The plan should include practical details (date, place, what will happen) and the request should be specific (collecting money for a gift, preparing a speech, contacting former staff).

materials.title: Essay: a four-day working week
materials.instructions: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
materials.prompt:
Some people believe that a four-day working week would be better for both employees and businesses.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
materials.scoringGuidance: Both "employees and businesses" should be addressed. Possible ideas: well-being and productivity, recruitment advantages, versus industries that need continuous cover, customer service and pay concerns. A partly agree position must still be clear and consistent.

materials.title: Essay: online learning or the classroom?
materials.instructions: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
materials.prompt:
Some people think that online courses are as effective as learning in a classroom. Others believe that face-to-face teaching is essential.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
materials.scoringGuidance: Balanced development of both views with a clear opinion. Strong answers distinguish between kinds of learners and subjects (self-motivated adults versus young children; theory versus practical skills such as laboratory work).

materials.title: Essay: who should reduce plastic packaging?
materials.instructions: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
materials.prompt:
The amount of plastic packaging used for food and other products is increasing.

Why is this happening? Who should be responsible for reducing it: governments, companies or individuals?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
materials.scoringGuidance: Both questions must be answered. Causes might include convenience, food safety and online shopping. The second answer needs a clear allocation of responsibility (it may be shared, but the writer should say who should lead and why).

materials.title: Part 1: weekends and free time
materials.instructions: The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question in two to four sentences.
speakingQuestions: What did you do last weekend?
Do you usually plan your weekends or decide at the last minute?
Is there anything new you would like to try at the weekend?
Do you prefer spending free time indoors or outdoors?
How did you spend weekends when you were a child?

materials.title: Part 1: shopping
materials.instructions: The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question in two to four sentences.
speakingQuestions: Do you prefer shopping online or in shops? Why?
What was the last thing you bought for yourself?
Are there any big shopping centres near where you live?
Do you ever buy second-hand things?

materials.title: Part 2: a memorable journey
materials.instructions: You will have one minute to prepare. You can make notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.
materials.prompt: Describe a journey you remember well.
bullets: and explain why you remember this journey
materials.scoringGuidance: Narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect) and sequencing language support Grammatical Range and Coherence. Focus on one or two vivid moments rather than a full itinerary.

materials.title: Part 2: an achievement you are proud of
materials.instructions: You will have one minute to prepare. You can make notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.
materials.prompt: Describe something you achieved that made you proud.
bullets: and explain why it made you proud

materials.title: Part 3: travel and tourism
materials.instructions: The examiner asks you more general questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Give developed answers with reasons and examples.
speakingQuestions: Why do people enjoy travelling to other countries?
How has tourism changed the place where you live?
Should tourists pay extra taxes to visit popular places?
Do you think people will travel more or less in the future?

materials.title: Part 3: success and ambition
materials.instructions: The examiner asks you more general questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Give developed answers with reasons and examples.
speakingQuestions: How do people in your country usually define success?
Is it better to set ambitious goals or realistic ones?
Do young people today face more pressure to succeed than in the past?
Should schools reward effort as well as results?
